title: Michael Collins, the Man Who Stayed Behind
text:
On 20 July 1969, while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the Moon and walked on its surface, the third member of the Apollo 11 crew, Michael Collins, stayed in lunar orbit aboard the command module Columbia. Hundreds of millions of people watched the moonwalk on television. Collins could not; he had no television picture.

His job was less visible but no less essential. Columbia was the crew's only way home. Collins had to keep it working, track the lunar module, and be ready to fly down and rescue his crewmates if their ascent went wrong. He carried a thick notebook of contingency plans for different rendezvous problems. Each time Columbia passed behind the Moon he was out of radio contact with everyone, alone on the far side.

In his memoir, Carrying the Fire, Collins wrote that he did not feel lonely during those passes but rather a sense of awareness and even joy. His real fear, he said, was that Armstrong and Aldrin might be stranded, and that he would have to fly home alone, a marked man for the rest of his life.

They were not stranded. On 21 July Eagle lifted off, Collins guided the docking, and the three men flew home together. Collins later turned down the chance to command a future Moon landing and left NASA. He never walked on the Moon, and he said he did not regret it.
lesson: Every team depends on roles that get little attention. Doing the unseen job well is what lets the visible work happen.
people: Michael Collins, Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin
source: Michael Collins, Carrying the Fire (1974); NASA Apollo 11 mission records
